claim: Tardigrades are microscopic animals renowned for their ability to withstand extreme conditions, including high doses of ionizing radiation (IR).
source: Tardigrades are microscopic animals renowned for their ability to withstand extreme conditions, including high doses of ionizing radiation (IR).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific knowledge about tardigrades.

claim: The rate of single-strand breaks induced in H. exemplaris was roughly equivalent to that in human cells.
source: Importantly, we found that the rate of single-strand breaks induced was roughly equivalent to that in human cells, suggesting that DNA repair plays a predominant role in tardigrades' radio-resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing SSB rates between tardigrades and human cells as described in the manuscript.

claim: TDR1 is a novel tardigrade-specific gene that is strongly overexpressed in response to ionizing radiation in three different tardigrade species.
source: In all three species, many DNA repair genes were among the most strongly overexpressed genes alongside a novel tardigrade-specific gene, which we named Tardigrade DNA damage Response 1 (TDR1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptomics data across three species showing TDR1 upregulation.

claim: TDR1 protein interacts with DNA and forms aggregates at high concentration.
source: We found that TDR1 protein interacts with DNA and forms aggregates at high concentration suggesting it may condensate DNA and preserve chromosome organization until DNA repair is accomplished.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experimental data showing DNA-binding and aggregate formation.

claim: When expressed in human cells, TDR1 improved resistance to Bleomycin, a radiomimetic drug.
source: Remarkably, when expressed in human cells, TDR1 improved resistance to Bleomycin, a radiomimetic drug.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human cell culture experiments.

claim: Tardigrades belong to the clade of ecdysozoans, which also includes nematodes and arthropods.
source: With over 1400 species, they belong to the clade of ecdysozoans, which also includes nematodes and arthropods (Degma and Roberto, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Many species across the Tardigrada phylum can tolerate irradiation doses higher than 4000 Gy.
source: Many species across the Tardigrada phylum can tolerate irradiation doses higher than 4000 Gy (Hashimoto and Kunieda, 2017), but some are less tolerant, like Echiniscoides sigismundi, which has an LD50 at 48 hr of 1000 Gy (Jönsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The maximum dose compatible with maintenance of fertility in H. exemplaris is 100 Gy.
source: However, the doses compatible with maintenance of fertility seem much lower, e.g., the maximum is 100 Gy for Hypsibius exemplaris (Beltrán-Pardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Dsup is a tardigrade-specific gene that encodes an abundant chromatin protein that increases resistance to X-rays when expressed in human cells.
source: For resistance to IR, the tardigrade-specific gene Dsup (for DNA damage suppressor) has been discovered in Ramazzottius varieornatus. Dsup encodes an abundant chromatin protein that increases resistance to X-rays when expressed in human cells (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: DNA damage induced by hydroxyl radicals was reduced when Dsup was added to nucleosomal DNA in vitro.
source: In vitro experiments have shown that DNA damage induced by hydroxyl radicals was reduced when Dsup was added to nucleosomal DNA (Chavez et al., 2019), indicating DNA protection by Dsup.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: It is not yet possible to inactivate genes with CRISPR-Cas9 in tardigrades.
source: However, it is not yet possible to inactivate genes with CRISPR-Cas9 in tardigrades (Goldstein, 2022) and direct evidence for the importance of Dsup in radio-resistance of tardigrades is still lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In rotifers, the rate of DNA double-strand breaks is equivalent to that in human cells.
source: In rotifers, the rate of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is equivalent to that in human cells (Gladyshev and Meselson, 2008), showing that DNA repair, rather than DNA protection, plays a predominant role in their radio-resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Genes of DNA repair are upregulated in response to IR in rotifers and P. vanderplanki larvae.
source: Furthermore, it was recently found that genes of DNA repair are upregulated in response to IR in rotifers and P. vanderplanki larvae (Moris et al., 2023; Ryabova et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Irradiation with IR increases expression of Rad51 in Milnesium inceptum.
source: Previous studies have suggested that upregulation of DNA repair genes may also play a role in radio-resistance of tardigrades: irradiation with IR increases expression of Rad51, the canonical recombinase of homologous recombination (HR), in Milnesium inceptum (Beltrán-Pardo et al., 2013), and regulation of DNA repair genes was observed in R. varieornatus (Yoshida et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of H2AX is a universal response to DSBs in eukaryotes from yeast to humans.
source: In eukaryotes, from yeast to humans, phosphorylation of H2AX is a universal response to DSBs and an early step in the DNA repair process (Fernandez-Capetillo et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: H. exemplaris tardigrades were exposed to either 100 Gy or 1000 Gy of 137Cs γ-rays, which are known to be well tolerated by this species.
source: H. exemplaris tardigrades were exposed to either 100 Gy or 1000 Gy of 137Cs γ-rays, which are known to be well tolerated by this species (Beltrán-Pardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: For both 100 Gy and 1000 Gy doses, phospho-H2AX was detected at 30 min after irradiation, reached its peak levels at 4 hr and 8h30 and then gradually decreased.
source: For both 100 Gy and 1000 Gy doses, phospho-H2AX was detected at 30 min after irradiation, reached its peak levels at 4 hr and 8h30 and then gradually decreased (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Intense, ubiquitous phospho-H2AX labeling was observed in nuclei 4 hr after 100 Gy irradiation, which had significantly decreased 24 hr later.
source: Next, we performed whole-mount immunolabeling of tardigrades and observed intense, ubiquitous phospho-H2AX labeling in nuclei 4 hr after 100 Gy irradiation, which had significantly decreased 24 hr later (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: After 1000 Gy irradiation, the intense signal detected at 4 hr had decreased in most nuclei at 24 hr but it persisted at high intensity specifically in gonads.
source: After 1000 Gy irradiation, the intense signal detected at 4 hr had decreased in most nuclei at 24 hr but it persisted at high intensity specifically in gonads (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: The finding of persistent DSBs in gonads at 72 hr after 1000 Gy likely explains why H. exemplaris no longer lay eggs and become sterile after exposure to 1000 Gy.
source: The finding of persistent DSBs in gonads at 72 hr after 1000 Gy likely explains why H. exemplaris no longer lay eggs and become sterile after exposure to 1000 Gy (Beltrán-Pardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed persistent DSBs in gonads and is supported by a citation about sterility.

claim: DNA synthesis induced during DNA repair remained at low, undetectable levels in irradiated tardigrades.
source: In contrast, we could not detect any specific signal in irradiated tardigrades compared to controls, suggesting (i) that DNA synthesis induced during DNA repair remained at low, undetectable levels and (ii) that dividing intestinal cells detected in control animals were irreversibly damaged by the 1000 Gy irradiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: 1000 Gy induces irreversible damage in the gonads and dividing intestinal cells.
source: Phospho-H2AX immunolabeling experiments also suggested that 1000 Gy induces irreversible damage in the gonads and dividing intestinal cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on phospho-H2AX immunolabeling data.

claim: At 30 min after 1000 Gy irradiation, intensity of the high molecular weight band was drastically reduced, and DNA detected in the smear between 10 kb and 20 kb was strongly increased, indicating that 1000 Gy IR induces high rates of SSBs.
source: At 30 min after 1000 Gy irradiation, intensity of the high molecular weight band was drastically reduced, and DNA detected in the smear between 10 kb and 20 kb was strongly increased. In addition, the discrete band could no longer be detected. This clearly indicates that 1000 Gy IR induces high rates of SSBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by denaturing agarose gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The rate of SSB induction is approximately 0.05–0.1 SSB/Mb/Gy.
source: Considering that the majority of DNA fragments detected had a size of 10–20 kb and that the discrete band of 10–20 kb could no longer be detected, we can roughly evaluate that there is approximately 1 SSB every 10–20 kb. This corresponds to induction of SSBs at a rate of 0.05–0.1 SSB/Mb/Gy.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on analysis of DNA fragment sizes from gel electrophoresis data.

claim: SSBs are progressively repaired within 24–73 hr after irradiation.
source: Between 4 hr and 24 hr, the DNA migration profile was progressively restored and between 24 hr and 73 hr, it was identical to controls. Similar results were observed with the 100 Gy dose (Figure 1c). However, compared to 1000 Gy, the changes observed were not as marked and the discrete 10–20 kb band could always be detected, indicating SSBs were induced at lower rates. These results indicate that SSBs are inflicted by IR in a dose-dependent manner, roughly estimated to 0.05–0.1 SSB/Mb/Gy, and progressively repaired within the next 24–73 hr (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by denaturing agarose gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 421 genes were overexpressed more than 4-fold (with an adjusted p-value<0.05) in H. exemplaris 4 hr after irradiation, including 120 overexpressed more than 16-fold.
source: The analysis revealed that 421 genes were overexpressed more than 4-fold (with an adjusted p-value<0.05) including 120 overexpressed more than 16-fold (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of overexpressed genes highlighted a strong enrichment of DNA repair genes.
source: The Gene Ontology analysis of overexpressed genes highlighted a strong enrichment of DNA repair genes (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Genes for both major pathways of DNA DSB repair, HR and NHEJ, were among the most strongly stimulated genes.
source: In particular, genes for both major pathways of DNA DSB repair, HR and NHEJ, were among the most strongly stimulated genes. Examples are genes for RAD51 and MACROH2A1 in HR (Khurana et al., 2014; Baumann and West, 1998) and XRCC5 and XRCC6 in NHEJ (Doherty and Jackson, 2001; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data and citations to published literature.

claim: The gene for POLQ, the key player of the alternative end joining pathway of DNA DSB repair, was strongly upregulated.
source: The gene for POLQ, the key player of the alternative end joining pathway of DNA DSB repair (Mateos-Gomez et al., 2015), was also strongly upregulated (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data and a citation to published literature.

claim: Genes for XRCC1, PNKP, and LIG1 in base excision repair were among the most strongly overexpressed genes.
source: Also notable among most strongly overexpressed genes were genes for XRCC1, PNKP, and LIG1 in base excision repair (Whitehouse et al., 2001; Krokan and Bjørås, 2013), along with genes for PARP2 and PARP3, which catalyze PARylation of many DNA repair proteins (Pascal, 2018) and RNF146 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data and citations to published literature.

claim: RNF146 is a ubiquitin ligase that has been reported to be important for tolerance to IR in human cells by targeting PARylated XRCC5, XRCC6, and XRCC1 for degradation.
source: Interestingly, RNF146 is a ubiquitin ligase that has been reported to be important for tolerance to IR in human cells by targeting PARylated XRCC5, XRCC6, and XRCC1 for degradation (Kang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RNF146 upregulation could contribute to the remarkable resistance of tardigrades to IR.
source: Our results suggest that RNF146 upregulation could contribute to the remarkable resistance of tardigrades to IR.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observed upregulation of RNF146 and its known function in human cells.

claim: AMNP gene family members were observed among overexpressed genes.
source: Among overexpressed genes, we also observed AMNP gene family members (Yoshida et al., 2022) (one representative was labeled AMNP-like, Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data and a citation to published literature.

claim: AMNP genes encode tardigrade-specific Mn-peroxidases which are overexpressed in response to desiccation and UVC in R. varieornatus.
source: AMNP genes encode recently discovered tardigrade-specific Mn-peroxidases which are overexpressed in response to desiccation and UVC in R. varieornatus (Yoshida et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: AMNP gene g12777 was shown to increase tolerance to oxidative stress when expressed in human cells.
source: AMNP gene g12777 was shown to increase tolerance to oxidative stress when expressed in human cells (Yoshida et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: AMNP genes could contribute to resistance to IR by increasing tolerance to the associated oxidative stress.
source: Based on our results, it is possible that AMNP genes such as the AMNP-like gene identified here could contribute to resistance to IR by increasing tolerance to the associated oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observed upregulation of AMNP genes and their known function.

claim: H. exemplaris tardigrades survived for several days in the presence of 100 μM Bleomycin.
source: In preliminary experiments, we found that H. exemplaris tardigrades survived for several days in the presence of 100 μM Bleomycin, suggesting that H. exemplaris could resist chronic genotoxic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The correlation between highly expressed genes after IR and after Bleomycin treatment was strong for most upregulated DNA repair genes.
source: As expected, the correlation between highly expressed genes after IR and after Bleomycin treatment (with baseMean>500, Figure 2c and Figure 2—source data 3) was strong for most upregulated DNA repair genes such as XRCC5, XRCC6, PARP2, PARP3, XRCC1, LIG4, LIG1, and RNF146 (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptomics data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: TDR1 is a novel tardigrade-specific gene.
source: One such gene, which we named TDR1 (for Tardigrade DNA damage Response 1), was chosen for further investigation. Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) long read sequencing and cDNA cloning of TDR1 allowed us to determine the predicted TDR1 protein sequence which is 146 amino acids long (Supplementary files 1 and 2). We observed that the current genome assembly predicts a partially truncated TDR1 protein sequence, BV898_14257, due to an assembly error (Supplementary file 1). Our BLAST analysis against NCBI nucleotide non-redundant database suggested that TDR1 is a novel tardigrade-specific gene as no homolog could be found in any other ecdysozoan (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and BLAST searches.

claim: TDR1 protein was only detected after the induction of DNA damage.
source: Remarkably, similar to phospho-H2AX, TDR1 was only detected after the induction of DNA damage (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: XRCC5 and XRCC6 protein levels were stimulated by both Bleomycin and IR treatments, although the fold stimulation was much lower than at the RNA level.
source: XRCC5 and XRCC6 protein levels were also stimulated by both Bleomycin and IR treatments, although the fold stimulation was much lower than at the RNA level (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: He-Dsup expression remained stable at the protein level after the induction of DNA damage.
source: Furthermore, we checked expression of He-Dsup homolog in H. exemplaris (Chavez et al., 2019), which remained constant at the RNA level (see BV898_01301, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), and found that it also remained stable at the protein level after the induction of DNA damage (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3a and RNA sequencing data.

claim: More than 5600 proteins could be detected in all conditions by mass spectrometry-based quantitative proteomics.
source: More than 5600 proteins could be detected in all conditions (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: 58, 266, and 185 proteins were found to be differentially abundant at 4 hr post-irradiation, 24 hr post-irradiation, and after Bleomycin treatment, respectively.
source: Among them, 58, 266, and 185 proteins were found to be differentially abundant at 4 hr post-irradiation, 24 hr post-irradiation, and after Bleomycin treatment, respectively compared to control tardigrades (Log2 Fold Change>0.3 and limma p-value<0.01, leading to a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR<3%, Figure 3b, Table 1, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3b and Table 1.

claim: There was a good correlation between stimulation at RNA and protein levels.
source: We observed a good correlation between stimulation at RNA and protein levels (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA sequencing and proteomics data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Four different TDR1-related peptides were detected by mass spectrometry, providing direct evidence of strong TDR1 overexpression in response to IR.
source: Importantly, despite the small size of the predicted TDR1 protein, we detected four different TDR1-related peptides, providing direct evidence of strong TDR1 overexpression in response to IR (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: A. antarcticus and P. fairbanksi readily survived exposure to 1000 Gy.
source: We found by visual inspection of animals after IR that A. antarcticus and P. fairbanksi readily survived exposure to 1000 Gy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: TDR1 homologs were among the most overexpressed genes after IR in both A. antarcticus and P. fairbanksi.
source: Crucially, we identified TDR1 homologs in transcriptomes of A. antarcticus and P. fairbanksi and just like in H. exemplaris, these TDR1 homologs were among the most overexpressed genes after IR in both species and in response to Bleomycin treatment of A. antarcticus (Table 2, Figure 4—source data 1–3), strongly suggesting a conserved role of TDR1 in resistance to IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from multiple species.

claim: A Dsup homolog was identified in A. antarcticus but not in P. fairbanksi.
source: In contrast, as expected from previous studies, we could identify a Dsup homolog in A. antarcticus (Aant_geneID_rb_14333, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2), from the Hypsibioidea superfamily, but not in P. fairbanksi from Macrobiotoidea.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of transcriptomes.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of overexpressed genes highlighted a robust enrichment of DNA repair genes in A. antarcticus and P. fairbanksi in response to IR.
source: Furthermore, similar to H. exemplaris, Gene Ontology analysis of overexpressed genes highlighted a robust enrichment of DNA repair genes in A. antarcticus and P. fairbanksi in response to IR (Supplementary file 5a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: A high proportion of genes of the main repair pathways of DNA damages caused by IR were significantly overexpressed after IR in all three species.
source: Notably, a high proportion of genes of the main repair pathways of DNA damages caused by IR (DSB and SSB repair, and base excision repair) were significantly overexpressed after IR in all three species (Supplementary file 5c and d) and as in H. exemplaris, among the genes with the strongest overexpression in A. antarcticus and P. fairbanksi, we observed the canonical DNA repair genes for XRCC5, XRCC6, XRCC1, PARP2, PARP3, as well as the gene for RNF146.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from multiple species.

claim: A set of 50 putative orthologous genes was upregulated in response to IR in all three species.
source: Interestingly, a set of 50 putative orthologous genes was upregulated in response to IR in all three species, suggesting a conserved signaling and transcriptional program is involved in response to IR between the distantly related Hypsibioidea and Macrobiotoidea superfamilies (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: TDR1 proteins contain a relatively high proportion of basic amino acid residues (20.5% of K or R amino acids for TDR1 of H. exemplaris).
source: Interestingly, TDR1 proteins contain a relatively high proportion of basic amino acid residues (20.5% of K or R amino acids for TDR1 of H. exemplaris, He-TDR1), including at conserved positions in the C-terminal domain (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: When circular or linear plasmid DNA was incubated with increasing concentrations of He-TDR1, a shift in plasmid mobility was detected in agarose gel electrophoresis, indicating the formation of a complex between He-TDR1 and DNA.
source: As shown in Figure 5b and c, when circular or linear plasmid DNA was incubated with increasing concentrations of He-TDR1, a shift in plasmid mobility was detected in agarose gel electrophoresis, indicating the formation of a complex between He-TDR1 and DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: The observed binding of He-TDR1 at a ratio of 1 He-TDR1 protein to every 3 bp of DNA is similar to the binding reported for non-sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins such as the Rad51 recombinase.
source: The observed binding of He-TDR1 at a ratio of 1 He-TDR1 protein to every 3 bp of DNA is similar to the binding reported for non-sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins such as the Rad51 recombinase (Zaitseva et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to published literature.

claim: At high He-TDR1 concentrations, He-TDR1 and DNA form aggregates that could not enter the gel.
source: As an alternative explanation, we considered that at high He-TDR1 concentrations, He-TDR1 and DNA might form aggregates that could not enter the gel. To explore this possibility, we examined mixes of He-TDR1-GFP and plasmid DNA by fluorescence microscopy. At ratios at which complex formation was detected by agarose gel electrophoresis (Figure 5b and c), we observed fluorescent spots in the samples, suggesting the presence of large protein-DNA aggregates (of 2–5 µm) likely unable to enter the agarose gels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel shift assay and fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5b, c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: He-TDR1-mNeonGreen was predominantly localized to nuclei in tardigrade cells.
source: He-TDR1-mNeonGreen was easily detected in muscle cells, likely due to high muscle-specific activity of the He-Actin promoter, and predominantly localized to nuclei, as observed by confocal microscopy (Figure 5d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5d and e.

claim: He-TDR1 co-localized with Hoechst staining, suggesting He-TDR1 is able to interact with DNA in vivo.
source: Importantly, He-TDR1 co-localized with Hoechst staining, suggesting He-TDR1 is able to interact with DNA in vivo.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on confocal microscopy data showing co-localization.

claim: Expression of RvDsup-GFP and HeRNF146-GFP respectively reduced the number of phospho-H2AX foci in human U2OS cells treated with Bleomycin.
source: As previously demonstrated for RvDsup (Hashimoto et al., 2016) and as expected from the characterization of human RNF146 (Kang et al., 2011), expression of RvDsup-GFP and HeRNF146-GFP respectively reduced the number of phospho-H2AX foci.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to published literature.

claim: HeRNF146 is a homolog of human RNF146.
source: This result strongly suggests that HeRNF146 is a homolog of human RNF146.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on functional similarity observed in experiments.

claim: Expression of TDR1-GFP fusion proteins from all species tested significantly reduced the number of phospho-H2AX foci in human cells treated with Bleomycin.
source: Moreover, expression of TDR1-GFP fusion proteins from all species tested also significantly reduced the number of phospho-H2AX foci in human cells treated with Bleomycin, supporting the potential role of TDR1 proteins in tardigrade resistance to IR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human cell culture experiments.

claim: He-TDR1-GFP protein was localized in the nucleus of transfected human cells.
source: Figure 6b shows that He-TDR1-GFP protein was localized in the nucleus of transfected cells, which is consistent with its ability to directly interact with DNA and its nuclear localization after transgenic expression in H. exemplaris.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: DNA repair plays a major role in the radio-resistance of tardigrades.
source: Our results indicate that DNA repair plays a major role in the radio-resistance of tardigrades and identified the gene for TDR1, a novel DNA-binding protein highly upregulated in response to IR and likely to play an original function in DNA repair.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: The rate of SSB induction in H. exemplaris (0.05–0.1 SSB/Gy/Mb) is roughly similar to that reported for cultured human cells (0.17 SSB/Gy/Mb).
source: Using standard agarose gel electrophoresis, we were able to observe that SSBs were induced every 10–20 kb in H. exemplaris after exposure to 1000 Gy of γ-rays, indicating a rate of 0.05–0.1 SSB/Gy/Mb (Figure 1c). Remarkably, this rate is roughly similar to that reported for cultured human cells which is 0.17 SSB/Gy/Mb (Mohsin Ali et al., 2004), showing that high levels of DNA damage are induced after high doses of IR and thus supporting the importance of DNA repair in the radio-resistance of H. exemplaris compared to human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to published literature.

claim: The strongest upregulations, both at RNA and protein levels, were detected for proteins acting early in DNA repair in the different pathways involved.
source: Remarkably, the strongest upregulations, both at RNA and protein levels, were detected for proteins acting early in DNA repair in the different pathways involved: XRCC5/XRCC6 in NHEJ (Doherty and Jackson, 2001), POLQ in micro-homology-mediated end joining (MMEJ), XRCC1 in SSB, and PARP2/PARP3 which act as DNA damage sensors common to all DSB repair pathways (Pandey and Black, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing and proteomics data, along with citations to published literature.

claim: Producing higher amounts of early acting DNA repair proteins is essential to maintain DNA ends long enough for more limiting components of DNA repair to cope with an exceptionally high number of damages.
source: These early acting proteins either stabilize DNA ends or provide essential scaffolding for subsequent steps of DNA repair. It is possible that producing higher amounts of such proteins is essential to maintain DNA ends long enough for more limiting components of DNA repair to cope with an exceptionally high number of damages.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observed upregulation of early acting DNA repair proteins.

claim: XRCC5 and XRCC6 protein levels are regulated by a dynamic balance of synthesis, promoted by increased gene transcription, and degradation, made possible by RNF146 upregulation.
source: To explain the more modest fold stimulation of XRCC5 and XRCC6 at protein levels compared to its massive increase at mRNA levels, it is therefore tempting to speculate that, XRCC5 and XRCC6 protein levels (and perhaps that of other scaffolding complexes of DNA repair) are regulated by a dynamic balance of synthesis, promoted by increased gene transcription, and degradation, made possible by RNF146 upregulation.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observed discrepancy between RNA and protein levels and the known function of RNF146.

claim: Similar to human RNF146, He-RNF146 expression in human cells reduced the number of phospho-H2AX foci detected in response to Bleomycin.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that, similar to human RNF146 (Kang et al., 2011), He-RNF146 expression in human cells reduced the number of phospho-H2AX foci detected in response to Bleomycin (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and a citation to published literature.

claim: TDR1 may favor DNA repair by regulating chromosomal organization.
source: Proteins directly involved in DNA repair, however, usually accumulate at sites of DNA damage (Rothkamm et al., 2015), which did not appear to be the case for TDR1 overexpressed in human cells. Given that TDR1 can form aggregates with DNA in vitro, we speculate that it may favor DNA repair by regulating chromosomal organization.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the observed properties of TDR1 and a citation to published literature.

claim: The DNA-binding activities of TDR1 are reminiscent of DdrC from D. radiodurans.
source: Intriguingly, the DNA-binding activities of TDR1 are reminiscent of DdrC from D. radiodurans. DrdC is a small DNA-binding protein which is among the most strongly overexpressed proteins after irradiation of D. radiodurans with γ-rays (Tanaka et al., 2004) and DdrC forms aggregates with DNA in vitro (Banneville et al., 2022; Bouthier de la Tour et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on similarities between TDR1 and DdrC, supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Compared to Dsup, which has only been found in Hypsibioidea, TDR1 appears more widely present and could be a more ancient tardigrade gene.
source: The C-terminal portion of TDR1 is conserved in species of Macrobiotoidea and Hypsibioidea superfamilies of the Parachela order of Eutardigrada but absent from M. inceptum, the only representative of the Apochela order of Eutardigrada for which transcriptomic data is currently available (Supplementary file 6), and from Heterotardigrada. Compared to Dsup, which has only been found in Hypsibioidea, TDR1 appears more widely present and could be a more ancient tardigrade gene.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on phylogenetic distribution of TDR1 and Dsup.

claim: H. exemplaris (strain Z151) was cultivated in mineral water at 16°C with a 14 hr day and 10 hr night cycle and fed with Chlorella vulgaris microalgae.
source: H. exemplaris (strain Z151, Sciento, UK) and A. antarcticus (Giovannini et al., 2018) were cultivated from one individual in mineral water (Volvic, France) at 16°C with a 14 hr day and 10 hr night cycle and fed with Chlorella vulgaris microalgae from Algothèque MNHN, France, or ordered from https://www.ldc-algae.com/ (Greenbloom pure fresh Chlorella).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Tardigrades were exposed to a 137Cs γ-ray source at a dose rate of 12.74 Gy/min or 16 Gy/min for a total dose of 100 Gy or 1000 Gy.
source: For ionizing irradiations, tardigrades were exposed to a 137Cs γ-ray source (GSR-D1 irradiator, RPS Services Limited) at a dose rate of 12.74 Gy/min or 16 Gy/min for a total dose of 100 Gy or 1000 Gy.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Antibodies were raised against H. exemplaris proteins in rabbits by injecting selected peptide sequences.

claim: Recombinant He-TDR1 and He-TDR1-GFP were purified using Ni Sepharose affinity chromatography followed by gel filtration.
source: He-TDR1 and He-TDR1-GFP (see plasmid sequence in Supplementary file 2) were transformed in E. coli Rosetta 2(DE3). Single competent cells (Novagen, MerckMillipore). Protein expression was induced with 1 mM IPTG at OD600=0.6–0.7 in 2xYT medium (containing 50 µg/mL carbenicillin, 35 µg/mL chloramphenicol, and 1% glucose) at 25°C during 20 hr. Cells were resuspended in lysis buffer 25 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 500 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 1 mM TCEP (supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail [Roche]), and lysed by sonication (Vibracell 75186- 7 s ON/7 s OFF, 50% amplitude, 10 min). The first step of purification was binding on Ni Sepharose 6 Fast Flow resin in batch (overnight at 4°C). After binding, the resin was washed with lysis buffer and the protein was eluted with 25 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 500 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol, 1 mM TCEP. Eluted protein is concentrated (Amicon Ultra 10K) and diluted in buffer 25 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM TCEP. The second step of purification was a gel filtration Superdex 200 increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) equilibrated with 25 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM TCEP using AKTA Pure instrument (Cytiva).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Expression plasmids for TDR1-GFP fusion proteins were transfected into human U2OS cells by Amaxa electroporation.
source: Expression plasmids for fusion proteins of GFP and tardigrade proteins were constructed by Gibson assembly into pEGFP-N1 (Clontech) of the tardigrade cDNA (obtained by gene synthesis from Integrated DNA) or ordered from TwistBiosciences. Full nucleotide sequences of fusion proteins are provided as supplementary information (Supplementary file 2). Plasmids were transfected into human U2OS cells (purchased from ATCC ref ATCC-HTB-96 and regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination) by Amaxa electroporation with Nucleofector Kit V (Lonza) and plated in six-well plates containing glass slides.
